# NON-UNIQUENESS OF LERAY SOLUTIONS OF THE FORCED NAVIER-STOKES EQUATIONS

DALLAS ALBRITTON, ELIA BRUÉ, AND MARIA COLOMBO

ABSTRACT. In the seminal work [39], Leray demonstrated the existence of global weak solutions to the Navier-Stokes equations in three dimensions. We exhibit two distinct Leray solutions with zero initial velocity and identical body force Our approach is to construct a 'background' solution which is unstable for the Navier-Stokes dynamics in similarity variables; its similarity profile is a smooth, compactly supported vortex ring whose cross-section is a modification of the unstable two-dimensional vortex constructed by Vishik in [43, 44]. The second solution is a trajectory on the unstable manifold associated to the background solution, in accordance with the predictions of Jia and Sverák in [32, 33]. Our solutions live precisely on the borderline of the known well-posedness theory.

## 1. INTRODUCTION

In the seminal work [39], Leray demonstrated the existence of global weak solutions to the three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations in the whole space:

$$
\begin{array}{l} \partial_ {t} u + u \cdot \nabla u - \Delta u + \nabla p = f \\ \operatorname {d i v} u = 0. \\ \end{array}
$$

（NS）

Leray's work, and in particular his compactness method, has become paradigmatic for the construction of global weak solutions to many nonlinear PDEs. His weak solutions, which he called solutions turbulent, are now known as Leray-Hopf solutions, recognizing also the contribution [30] of Hopf in bounded domains.

Do Leray-Hopf solutions, perhaps augmented with suitability, constitute an existence and uniqueness class for the Navier-Stokes equations? Since Leray's work, this has remained an important open problem in the theory of the Navier-Stokes equations, as discussed in [30, 37] and, in the past decade, [33] and [11, Problem 9]. In 1969, Ladyzhenskaya [37] already gave an example of non-uniqueness to (NS), though in a time-varying domain which degenerates as $t \rightarrow 0^{+}$ and with nonstandard boundary conditions and a force. In recent years, this problem has been revisited, and various works have influenced the community toward the expectation that uniqueness does not hold. We mention two of particular importance: First, Jia, Šverák, and Guillod [32, 33, 28] developed a program towards non-uniqueness and supported the missing steps with numerical evidence. Second, Buckmaster and Vicol [12] constructed non-unique distributional solutions of the Navier-Stokes equations with finite kinetic energy via the powerful method of convex integration. Despite several attempts and results obtained alongside these ideas, convex integration is at the present time far from reaching the minimum regularity (1.1) required to speak of Leray-Hopf solutions.

Remarkably, to our knowledge, there is no existing unstable solution in three dimensions suitable for our purposes, with or without forcing.

Self-similarity, instability, and non-uniqueness in the Navier-Stokes equations: Jia, Sverák, and Guillod's program [32, 33, 28]. Let $a_{0}\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{3}\setminus\{0\})$ be divergence free and scaling invariant and $\sigma\in\mathbb{R}$ be a size parameter. One may ask whether there exists a scaling invariant solution $u_{\sigma}$ with initial data $u_{0,\sigma}=\sigma a_{0}.$ For $|\sigma|\ll1,$ existence and uniqueness falls into the known perturbation theory of Koch and Tataru [35] in $\mathrm{BMO}^{-1},$ for example. For arbitrary size, existence was demonstrated in [32] via a new local-in-space smoothing estimate and Leray-Schauder degree theory (see [5] and the references it cites for a simplified approach). Thus, the self-similar solutions constructed in [32] with initial data $u_{0,\sigma}$ constitute a continuous-in-$\sigma$ branch connected to the origin, and non-uniqueness in the Cauchy problem for (NS) is conjectured in [33] to arise due to bifurcations within or from this class of solutions. $^{6}$ In [33], spectral conditions on the linearized operator $L_{\mathrm{ss}}^{(\sigma)}$ (that is, linearized around the profiles $U_{\sigma}$ ) are identified for such bifurcations to occur. Moreover, it is shown how to truncate the solutions to have finite energy without introducing a force (for this, it is roughly necessary to 'watch' the eigenvalue become unstable). One of the spectral conditions was verified numerically in [28] on certain axisymmetric examples with pure swirl initial datum.

One of the main difficulties in rigorous verification of the spectral condition in [33] is that the self-similar solutions are non-explicit. In our work, the inclusion of a force gives us the freedom to search for a more explicit unstable profile.

Convex integration. Buckmaster and Vicol [12] (see also [8]) demonstrated nonuniqueness of distributional solutions to the Cauchy problem for the Navier-Stokes equations via the convex integration method for any $L^{2}$ initial datum. Their proof introduces the important tool of intermittency and builds on the fundamental works for the Euler equations and the proof of the Onsager conjecture [31, 9] (see [11, 10] for further connections to fluid turbulence). The solutions of [12] have finite kinetic energy $( u\in L_{t}^{\infty}L_{x}^{2})$ but do not belong to the energy class (1.1); more generally, all known convex integration schemes are far from reaching the regularity $\nabla u\in L_{t,x}^{2}$ necessary to speak of Leray solutions.

Non-uniqueness of Leray solutions was instead proved in [16, 17] for the hypodissipative Navier-Stokes equations, namely, with the Laplacian in (NS) replaced by a fractional Laplacian $(-\Delta)^{\alpha}$ of order $\alpha<1/3$ . In forthcoming work [2] by the first and third authors, we demonstrate non-uniqueness of Leray solutions of the forced Navier-Stokes equations in two dimensions in the whole supercritical range $\alpha<1.$ As in the present work, our methods are based on self-similarity and instability.

Recently, convex integration was also used [14, 15] to demonstrate the sharpness of certain classical results, obtaining in particular non-uniqueness in $L_{t}^{q}L_{x}^{\infty},$ q<2, in any dimension d $\geq 2$ , and in $C_{t}L_{x}^{p},$ p<2, in dimension d=2, respectively.

Vortex filaments. Our vortex ring construction is partially inspired by, though rather different from, the works [26, 3] on vortex filaments. In those papers, existence and uniqueness were established for a class of Navier-Stokes solutions whose initial vorticity is a Dirac mass along a curve. The infinitesimal structure of these vortex filaments is the two-dimensional Lamb-Oseen vortex, whose stability was demonstrated in [27] (see also [23, 24]). We mention also [25], which, motivated by vortex rings, discusses analogies between the two-dimensional and axisymmetric without-swirl Navier-Stokes equations from the perspective of well-posedness.

Open problems. As mentioned above, the main task of this paper is to find an unstable (forced) Euler steady state. The steady state we choose is a perturbation of a particular (unforced) unstable vortex of Vishik whose construction is far from simple. Given the flexibility afforded by a force, it would be interesting to know how generic this instability is and to develop a general method for finding these unstable (forced) solutions. It is, moreover, an open problem to remove the force.

## 2. LINEAR INSTABILITY: FROM TWO DIMENSIONS TO AXISYMMETRY

2. 1. Spectral preliminaries. Let H be a Hilbert space and $L : D ( L ) \subset H \to H$ be closed and densely defined. Then $D ( L )$ is a Hilbert space with the graph norm. The basic theory of these operators is reviewed in [41, VIII: Unbounded Operators]. A simple criterion for self-adjointness is that ker $L+i$ and ker $L-i$ are trivial.

The resolvent set $\rho(L)$ consists of those $\lambda\in\mathbb{C}$ such that $\lambda-L:D(L)\rightarrow H$ is invertible. Its inverse $R(\lambda,L):H\to D(L)$ is known as the resolvent, and it is bounded by the open mapping theorem. The spectrum $\sigma(L)$ is the complement of the resolvent set. In our convention, the essential spectrum $\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(L)$ is the set of spectral values for which $\lambda-L$ is not Fredholm of index zero. $^{7}$ The essential spectrum is closed. Moreover, [34, Theorem 5.28] (see also the discussion in [34, Chapter 4, Section 6]) can be used to show that, in each connected component of $\mathbb{C}\backslash\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(L)$ , (i) $\lambda-L$ is not invertible everywhere, or (ii) $\lambda-L$ is invertible except at isolated points.

An operator $\boldsymbol{T}: D(\boldsymbol{L})\rightarrow H$ is relatively compact with respect to $\boldsymbol{L}$ if $\boldsymbol{T}$ is compact when $D(\boldsymbol{L})$ is considered with the graph norm. A key property is that relatively compact perturbations do not disturb the essential spectrum: $\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(\boldsymbol{L}+\boldsymbol{T})=\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(\boldsymbol{L})$ , see [34, Theorem 5.26].

We frequently use the following reasoning: Consider an operator $L$ as above whose essential spectrum is known to be contained in a half space $\left\{\mathrm{Re}\lambda\leq\mu\right\}$ . We perturb $L$ by a relatively compact perturbation $T$ , so that $\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(L+T)=\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(L)$ . Furthermore, we typically know that the perturbed operator $L+T$ is invertible for $\mathrm{Re}\lambda\gg1$ . Hence, the spectrum in $\left\{\mathrm{Re}\lambda>\mu\right\}$ consists of isolated points.
